title: Career Readiness
description: A practical playbook for landing a job and doing well once you have one: writing a resume that gets read, building and using a professional network, performing well in interviews, negotiating an offer with real numbers, and navigating your first year at a new job.
outcomes: You can write a resume with quantified, achievement-focused bullet points tailored to a specific job posting.
You can build and use a professional network, including a working LinkedIn profile and a plan for informational interviews.
You can answer behavioral interview questions using the STAR method with concrete, specific stories.
You can evaluate a job offer's total compensation and negotiate salary using researched numbers and a clear counter-offer approach.
You can navigate your first 90 days at a new job, build workplace relationships, and know when and how to make the case for a raise.

units.title: Building a Resume and Cover Letter That Get Read
units.summary: How applicant tracking systems and hiring managers actually screen resumes, and how to write bullet points and letters that survive both.

lessons.title: Resume Structure and the 6-Second Scan
lessons.intro: Studies of recruiter eye-tracking behavior have found an initial resume scan often lasts only a matter of seconds before a decision to read further, or not, starts forming. A resume built around that reality looks different from one built to be read carefully from top to bottom.

sections.heading: What Recruiters Actually Look At First
body: In that first fast scan, attention typically lands on contact information, the most recent job title, and the top one or two bullet points underneath it. If nothing there signals relevance to the role, the rest of the page may never get a careful read at all.

This is why the most relevant, most impressive material has to be positioned at the very top, and why resumes are built in reverse-chronological order, most recent experience first, since that's the section getting the most attention by default.

sections.heading: Choosing What to Include
body: A resume isn't a complete life history, it's a targeted argument for one specific job. Relevance should outweigh completeness: a job from years ago with no connection to the target role often belongs off the page entirely, or reduced to a single line, rather than expanded with detail nobody asked for.

For early-career candidates, one page is usually the right length; padding a thin resume with irrelevant detail to fill a second page tends to dilute the strong material rather than strengthen the overall impression.

sections.heading: Formatting for Humans and for ATS Software
body: Many employers run resumes through an applicant tracking system (ATS) before a human ever sees them, software that parses the document for keywords and formats it into a searchable record. A resume built with tables, text boxes, or unusual graphics can parse incorrectly or drop content entirely in some systems.

Using standard section headings (Experience, Education, Skills), a simple single-column layout, and a common file format keeps the document readable by both the software doing the first pass and the human doing the second.

keyTerms.def: Software that scans and organizes resumes by keyword before a human reviewer sees them.
Listing experience with the most recent role first, the standard resume structure.
The overlap between terms in a resume and terms in the job posting, used by both ATS software and human reviewers.
The typical length target for early-career resumes, prioritizing relevance over completeness.

practice.q: Why does the initial fast scan of a resume matter so much for how it's structured?
choices: Because resumes are only ever read once, in full
Because the most relevant material needs to be positioned where that brief initial scan naturally lands, or the rest may not get read carefully
Because recruiters never read past the first line regardless of content
Fast scans have no real influence on hiring decisions
practice.explain: Since the earliest attention is limited and predictable (contact info, recent title, top bullets), placing the strongest, most relevant material there increases the odds the rest gets a careful read.

practice.q: What is the main risk of formatting a resume with tables, text boxes, or decorative graphics?
choices: It always looks more professional to human reviewers
Some applicant tracking systems can misparse or drop content from those elements before a human ever sees it
ATS software cannot process any resume at all
There is no downside to unusual formatting
practice.explain: ATS software reads resumes as structured text; unusual layout elements like tables or text boxes can cause content to be misread or lost entirely during that automated parsing step.

practice.q: For an early-career candidate, what is generally the better approach: a padded two-page resume, or a focused one-page resume?
choices: The padded two-page resume, since more content is always better
The focused one-page resume, since padding with irrelevant detail tends to dilute the strongest, most relevant material
Length makes no difference to how a resume is received
A three-page resume covering every job ever held
practice.explain: For early-career candidates, a tight, relevant one-page resume typically outperforms a padded longer one, since irrelevant filler competes for attention with the material that actually matters.

lessons.title: Writing Achievement Bullets That Quantify Impact
lessons.intro: 'Responsible for handling customer complaints' describes a job description. 'Resolved 30+ customer complaints per week while maintaining a 95% satisfaction rating' describes a track record. The second version is built the same way every strong resume bullet is: with a number attached to a result.

sections.heading: Task Bullets vs Achievement Bullets
body: A task bullet describes a responsibility in passive, generic terms, it tells a reader what the job involved, which they can usually already guess from the job title alone. An achievement bullet describes a specific, measurable result you produced while doing that job, which is new information a title alone can't convey.

The reliable formula is action verb, plus what you did, plus a measurable result: start with a strong verb (led, built, resolved, reduced), describe the specific action, and close with a number or concrete outcome that shows the effect of that action.

sections.heading: Finding Numbers Even in 'Unquantifiable' Jobs
body: Almost every job has a countable element hiding in it, even without an obvious sales figure: hours worked, people served or trained, money or inventory handled, frequency of a task, or a percentage improvement in something measurable. When an exact number isn't remembered, a reasonable, honest estimate based on typical volume is generally acceptable, as long as it's not inflated beyond what actually happened.

The goal is reconstructing a plausible, defensible number from what you actually know about the role's scale, not inventing one, since a number you can't explain if asked in an interview does more harm than a bullet with no number at all.

example.problem: Turn this weak bullet into a strong, quantified one: 'Worked at campus coffee shop, helped customers and closed the register at night.'
steps: Identify the core actions performed: serving customers and handling closing/cash duties.
Estimate realistic numbers from the role's typical scale: the shop serves roughly 150 customers per weekday shift, and nightly cash reconciliation regularly exceeded $400.
Apply the formula: strong action verb, specific scope, measurable outcome.
Draft the bullet: 'Served an average of 150+ customers per shift and reconciled nightly cash drawers exceeding $400 with zero discrepancies over 6 months.'
example.answer: A bullet like 'Served 150+ customers per shift; reconciled $400+ in nightly cash with zero discrepancies over 6 months' reads as a track record with evidence, not just a description of what the job involved.

sections.heading: Matching Bullets to the Job Posting
body: Reading the job posting closely and mirroring its specific language, using 'cross-functional collaboration' if that's the posting's phrase for what you'd otherwise call 'working with other teams', helps both an ATS keyword scan and a human reviewer see the connection quickly.

This only works honestly when the underlying experience is real; mirroring language to describe something you didn't actually do crosses from tailoring into misrepresentation, which tends to surface quickly in an interview when asked for specifics.

keyTerms.def: A resume bullet describing a specific, measurable result rather than a general job responsibility.
A strong opening verb (led, built, reduced) that starts an achievement-focused resume bullet.
A number or measurable outcome included in a resume bullet to show the effect of an action.
Using the job posting's own specific language in a resume, when it honestly reflects real experience.

practice.q: Which of these is an achievement bullet rather than a task bullet?
choices: 'Responsible for managing social media accounts.'
'Grew Instagram following from 400 to 2,200 followers in 6 months through a weekly content calendar.'
'Helped with various marketing tasks.'
'Worked on the marketing team part-time.'
practice.explain: The second option names a specific action (a content calendar) and a measurable result (400 to 2,200 followers in 6 months), which is what distinguishes an achievement bullet from a generic task description.

practice.q: What is the recommended structure for a strong resume bullet?
choices: A long paragraph describing the entire job in detail
A strong action verb, a specific action taken, and a measurable result
The job title repeated with different wording
A list of every task performed during the role
practice.explain: The action-verb-plus-result formula keeps a bullet specific and evidence-based, rather than a vague or overly long description of general duties.

practice.q: When an exact number for an accomplishment isn't remembered, what is the recommended approach?
choices: Leave out any mention of scale or impact entirely
Invent an impressive-sounding number regardless of accuracy
Use a reasonable, honest estimate based on the role's typical scale, one you could explain if asked about it in an interview
Only include numbers that were officially recorded in writing
practice.explain: A defensible estimate based on real, typical scale is appropriate and far better than no number at all, but it must be honest enough to hold up if an interviewer asks how the number was calculated.

lessons.title: Writing a Cover Letter That Isn't Just a Repeated Resume
lessons.intro: A cover letter that just restates the resume in paragraph form wastes the one part of the application built specifically to say something the resume format can't: a direct explanation of why this particular job, at this particular company, matters to you.

sections.heading: What a Cover Letter Is Actually For
body: A resume lists what you've done; a cover letter connects that history to this specific opportunity, answering why this company, why this role, and why now, in a way a bulleted list can't. A letter that could be sent unchanged to any job posting has failed at that core purpose.

This means genuinely researching the company and role before writing is not optional; a letter demonstrating real, specific knowledge of what the company does and why it matters to you stands out precisely because most applicants skip this step.

sections.heading: The Three-Paragraph Structure
body: A workable structure has three parts. The opening paragraph names the specific role and gives one specific, genuine reason for interest in this company, not a generic compliment that could apply to any employer. The body paragraph tells one or two concrete stories from your background that connect directly to what the role actually needs.

The closing paragraph restates interest briefly and includes a clear, direct call to action, such as welcoming the opportunity to discuss the role further in an interview, rather than trailing off vaguely.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes That Get Letters Rejected
body: The most common mistake is a generic letter reused across every application with only the company name swapped, which is often detectable at a glance and signals low genuine interest. A close second is restating the resume's bullet points nearly verbatim in paragraph form, which adds nothing the resume didn't already say.

Focusing entirely on what you want from the job, rather than what you'd bring to it, and leaving in a leftover company name from a template used for a different application are both fast ways to get a letter set aside without a second read.

keyTerms.def: A letter accompanying a resume that connects your specific background to a specific role and company.
A clear closing statement inviting the next step, such as an interview.
Customizing a cover letter's content to the specific company and role rather than reusing generic text.
Reusing a cover letter across applications with minimal or no changes, a common reason letters get rejected.

practice.q: What is the main purpose of a cover letter that a resume's bulleted format doesn't already serve?
choices: Listing every job ever held in more detail
Directly explaining why this specific role and company matter to you, connecting your background to their specific needs
Repeating the resume's content in complete sentences
Providing references and contact information
practice.explain: A cover letter's unique value is making an explicit, specific connection between your background and this particular opportunity, something a resume's list format isn't built to do.

practice.q: Which opening line best reflects genuine, specific interest rather than a generic template?
choices: 'I am a hard worker who would be a great addition to any team.'
'I'm excited to apply for the Marketing Coordinator role at your company, given my strong work ethic.'
'Having followed your company's expansion into sustainable packaging over the past year, I'm excited to apply for the Marketing Coordinator role and contribute to that specific initiative.'
'To Whom It May Concern: please find my resume attached.'
practice.explain: The third option names a specific, real detail about the company that shows actual research and a genuine reason for interest, rather than a generic statement that could apply to any employer.

practice.q: What is one of the most common reasons cover letters get set aside without a careful read?
choices: Including a specific call to action at the end
Reusing a generic letter across multiple applications with little or no customization
Mentioning a real detail about the company's recent work
Keeping the letter to one page
practice.explain: A clearly generic, reused letter signals low genuine interest in the specific role and is one of the fastest ways to get set aside, compared to a letter that shows real, specific research.

units.title: Networking and Finding Opportunities
units.summary: Most jobs are filled through referrals rather than public postings alone, which makes building and using a network a learnable skill, not a fixed personality trait.

lessons.title: Why Networking Beats Cold Applications
lessons.intro: Submitting an application through a company website and waiting is the most common job-search strategy and, for most roles, one of the least effective on its own, since a large share of positions are filled through referrals and existing connections before, or instead of, ever being seriously sourced from that public pipeline.

sections.heading: The Hidden Job Market
body: A substantial share of hiring happens through what's sometimes called the hidden job market: roles filled through internal referrals, direct outreach, or word of mouth, sometimes without ever being posted publicly, or posted only after an internal or referred candidate is already being considered.

Referred candidates are also interviewed at meaningfully higher rates than candidates who apply cold through a general posting, since a referral carries an implicit vouching from someone already inside the organization, which a stranger's application can't provide on its own.

sections.heading: What Networking Actually Looks Like
body: Networking done well isn't asking a near-stranger for a favor, it's building genuine professional relationships over time, ones where value can flow in both directions, sharing a relevant article, making an introduction, or simply staying genuinely in touch, not only reaching out when something is needed.

This reframing matters because approaching networking as a transactional ask tends to feel uncomfortable and comes across that way; approaching it as building an ongoing professional relationship, with no immediate ask attached, tends to feel more natural and produces better long-term results.

sections.heading: Starting Where You Already Are
body: A real professional network usually already exists in some form: professors, past employers and coworkers, family friends, alumni from your school working in a field of interest, and members of clubs or organizations you're part of. These existing connections are typically easier to reach out to than a stranger, and often more willing to help.

The goal at the start isn't to reach dozens of new people immediately, it's to reconnect deliberately with a handful of people already in your circle and let that smaller network grow naturally from there.

keyTerms.def: Positions filled through referrals or internal connections, sometimes without ever being publicly posted.
A recommendation from someone already inside an organization, which increases a candidate's chance of being interviewed.
A brief, low-pressure conversation to learn about someone's career path or field, not a direct request for a job.
The set of professional relationships, including existing ones like professors or past coworkers, that can support a job search.

practice.q: Why does networking tend to outperform cold applications for many job searches?
choices: Because cold applications are never reviewed by anyone
Because a large share of positions are filled through referrals, and referred candidates are interviewed at meaningfully higher rates
Because networking guarantees a job offer
Because job postings are always fake
practice.explain: Referrals provide an implicit vouching that a cold application can't, which is why referred candidates are interviewed at higher rates even though cold applications remain a valid part of a job search.

practice.q: What is the recommended way to think about networking, according to this lesson?
choices: As asking near-strangers for favors as efficiently as possible
As building genuine, ongoing professional relationships where value can flow in both directions, not just a transactional ask
As something only useful for people who are naturally extroverted
As unnecessary if a resume is strong enough
practice.explain: Reframing networking as relationship-building rather than a one-time transactional request tends to feel more natural and produces better long-term results.

practice.q: Where does the lesson suggest starting when building a professional network?
choices: Only with senior executives at target companies
With people already in your existing circle, such as professors, past employers, or alumni
Exclusively through cold messages to strangers on social media
Only after already having several years of work experience
practice.explain: Existing connections are typically both easier to reach and more willing to help than complete strangers, making them the natural starting point for building out a network.

lessons.title: Informational Interviews and Building a LinkedIn Profile
lessons.intro: Asking someone directly for a job is a big, easy-to-decline request. Asking for 15 minutes of their time to learn about their career path is a small, easy-to-accept one, and it's often the request that eventually leads to the job anyway.

sections.heading: Requesting and Running an Informational Interview
body: A good request is short and specific: naming who you are, how you found them, and a clear, small ask, 15 to 20 minutes of their time to learn about their path into the field, with a specific reason you're reaching out to them in particular rather than a generic mass message.

During the conversation itself, useful questions focus on their actual career path, what a typical day in the role really involves, and what advice they'd give someone starting out, rather than asking directly for a job, which changes the nature of the conversation and can make the person you're talking to uncomfortable.

sections.heading: A LinkedIn Profile That Actually Works
body: A professional photo, a headline that says more than just a job title (what you actually do or are working toward, not only 'Student at University'), and an About section with a clear, brief pitch, who you are and what you're looking for, make a profile function as a real introduction rather than a bare directory listing.
The Experience section should mirror the achievement-focused bullets from your resume, specific and quantified where possible, rather than a shorter, vaguer version of the same content.

sections.heading: Staying in Touch Without Being Annoying
body: A short, specific thank-you note within 24 hours of an informational interview or a helpful conversation, referencing something specific that was discussed, makes a noticeably stronger impression than a generic thanks.

After that, light, occasional contact, an update a few months later, engaging genuinely with something they post, keeps the relationship warm without repeated direct asks, which is what makes reaching out again later, when there is a specific need, feel natural rather than sudden.

keyTerms.def: A brief conversation requesting insight into someone's career path, not a direct request for a job.
The short line under your name on LinkedIn, ideally describing what you do or seek, not just a job title.
A timely, specific message after a conversation or interview, referencing what was actually discussed.
Occasional, low-pressure contact that keeps a professional relationship active without repeated direct requests.

practice.q: What is the appropriate main goal of an informational interview request?
choices: Directly asking the contact for a job opening
Requesting a brief, specific amount of time to learn about their career path and advice for someone starting out
Asking them to review your resume line by line
Requesting an introduction to their entire team at once
practice.explain: An informational interview is framed around learning, not a direct job ask, which is a smaller, easier request for the other person to accept and tends to lead to stronger long-term relationships.

practice.q: Which LinkedIn headline better reflects the advice in this lesson?
choices: 'Student at University'
'Marketing student building data-driven campaign skills; seeking a summer internship in digital marketing'
'Looking for any job, please contact me'
Leaving the headline field blank
practice.explain: A strong headline says more than just a status or job title, giving a specific sense of what the person does or is working toward, which makes the profile function as a real introduction.

practice.q: What is 'light-touch contact' in the context of maintaining a professional network?
choices: Sending a job request every few weeks
Occasional, low-pressure contact, like sharing an update or engaging with a post, that keeps a relationship warm without repeated direct asks
Only contacting someone once and never again
Meeting in person exclusively, never online
practice.explain: Light-touch contact keeps a relationship active through small, low-pressure gestures over time, which makes a future direct ask feel natural rather than sudden or purely transactional.

lessons.title: Working a Career Fair and Following Up
lessons.intro: Walking up to a career fair table with no plan beyond 'see what's there' tends to produce a forgettable thirty-second exchange. A little preparation turns the same table into a genuine first conversation with someone who might remember your name the next day.

sections.heading: Preparing Before You Walk In
body: Researching 5 to 10 target companies in advance, what they do, what roles they're likely hiring for, lets you walk up with something specific to say rather than a generic opener. Preparing a 30-second self-introduction covering who you are, what you're studying or have done, and what you're looking for, sometimes called an elevator pitch, keeps the opening from feeling improvised.

Bringing printed copies of your resume, even in an increasingly digital hiring process, still matters at most career fairs, where a recruiter may want something physical to reference or hand off to a hiring manager afterward.

sections.heading: What to Say and Ask at the Table
body: Opening with the prepared self-introduction, then asking a specific, informed question, referencing something you learned in your research rather than a generic 'what does your company do,' signals real preparation and tends to produce a more substantive conversation.

Before moving to the next table, getting a name and a way to follow up, a business card, a LinkedIn connection, or an email, turns a brief conversation into something that can actually continue afterward.

sections.heading: The Follow-Up That Gets Remembered
body: A follow-up email sent within 48 hours, referencing the specific person's name and something particular from the conversation, stands out clearly against the generic 'nice to meet you' messages most recruiters receive after a career fair.
A short note like referencing a specific detail discussed at the table shows the conversation actually mattered, rather than being one of dozens of identical tables visited that day.

keyTerms.def: A prepared, roughly 30-second self-introduction covering who you are and what you're looking for.
An event where employers and job seekers meet directly, often through short table conversations.
A specific, individualized message after a conversation, referencing details actually discussed.
A prepared list of specific employers researched in advance of an event like a career fair.

practice.q: Why is researching 5 to 10 target companies before a career fair useful?
choices: It guarantees a job offer from one of them
It allows for specific, informed questions and conversation rather than a generic opener at each table
It is required by most career fair organizers
It replaces the need to bring a resume
practice.explain: Prior research lets a conversation move past generic small talk into something specific and memorable, which tends to leave a stronger impression than an unprepared exchange.

practice.q: Which question at a career fair table best reflects genuine preparation?
choices: 'What does your company do?'
'I saw you recently launched a new sustainability initiative, can you tell me more about how that team is structured?'
'Are you hiring?'
'Can I have a free pen?'
practice.explain: Referencing specific, researched information about the company signals real preparation and tends to produce a more substantive, memorable conversation than a generic question.

practice.q: What makes a career fair follow-up email more likely to be remembered by a recruiter?
choices: Sending it exactly one month later
Sending it within 48 hours and referencing a specific detail from the actual conversation
Copying the same generic message sent to every recruiter
Waiting for the recruiter to reach out first
practice.explain: A timely, specific follow-up referencing the actual conversation stands out against generic thank-you messages, which most recruiters receive in bulk after a career fair.

units.title: Interviewing and Negotiating the Offer
units.summary: Structured preparation for behavioral interview questions, and a way to evaluate and negotiate a job offer using real numbers instead of guessing.

lessons.title: The STAR Method for Behavioral Questions
lessons.intro: 'Tell me about a time you dealt with a difficult team member' isn't really asking about that one team member. It's asking how you're likely to handle a similar situation in this job, and a vague or hypothetical answer doesn't actually answer that underlying question.

sections.heading: Why 'Tell Me About a Time...' Questions Exist
body: Behavioral interview questions are built on the idea that specific past behavior predicts future behavior better than a hypothetical answer about what you'd do in theory. A candidate who answers with general opinions ('I believe in good communication') rather than a specific real example hasn't actually demonstrated anything.

This is why interviewers keep pushing for specifics, 'what exactly did you say,' 'what happened next', when an answer starts drifting toward the general or hypothetical; they're looking for real, concrete evidence of past behavior.

sections.heading: Situation, Task, Action, Result
body: STAR breaks a strong answer into four parts. Situation briefly sets the context, one or two sentences. Task names your specific responsibility or goal within that situation. Action, which should take up the majority of the answer, describes exactly what you specifically did, step by step. Result closes with the concrete outcome, ideally with a number attached.

A common mistake is spending most of the answer on Situation and Task, background and setup, and rushing through the Action, which is the part that actually shows what you did and how you think, and is what the interviewer is most trying to evaluate.

example.problem: Build a STAR answer to 'Tell me about a time you dealt with a difficult team member,' using this raw material: a group project worth 20% of the final grade, one member missed two deadlines, you proposed splitting the remaining work and setting up check-ins, the project was submitted on time and earned a B+.
steps: Situation, one sentence: a group project worth 20% of the final grade where one teammate missed two deadlines.
Task, one sentence: as the person who noticed the group falling behind, you needed to get the project back on track without escalating conflict.

Action, the bulk of the answer: describe specifically proposing a redistribution of remaining tasks, setting up short daily check-ins, and following up directly but respectfully with the struggling teammate.
Result, one to two sentences with a number: the project was submitted on time and earned a B+, and the teammate's participation improved for the rest of the semester.
example.answer: A tight STAR answer leads with one sentence of context, spends most of the time on the specific actions taken, and ends with a concrete, ideally quantified, result rather than a vague sense that things 'worked out.'

sections.heading: Building Your Story Bank Before the Interview
body: Preparing 5 to 6 flexible stories in advance, covering common themes like conflict, failure, leadership, and working under deadline pressure, means an interview question can be answered by adapting an already-thought-through story rather than trying to construct one from scratch in the moment.

The same underlying story can often be reshaped to answer several different questions depending on which part is emphasized, which is why a small set of well-prepared stories covers a surprisingly wide range of likely questions.

keyTerms.def: A structure for behavioral interview answers: Situation, Task, Action, Result.
An interview style based on the principle that specific past behavior predicts future behavior.
A prepared set of specific personal stories covering common interview themes, ready to be adapted to different questions.
A concrete, ideally numerical outcome used to close a STAR answer's Result section.

practice.q: Why do interviewers ask behavioral questions like 'tell me about a time...' instead of hypothetical questions like 'what would you do if...'?
choices: Hypothetical questions are considered unfair by most companies
Specific past behavior is considered a better predictor of future behavior than a hypothetical, untested answer
Behavioral questions are always shorter to answer
There is no meaningful difference between the two question types
practice.explain: Behavioral interviewing is built on the premise that real past actions predict future behavior more reliably than an answer describing what someone believes they would theoretically do.

practice.q: In a STAR answer, which part should typically take up the majority of the response?
choices: Situation
Task
Action
All four parts should be given exactly equal time
practice.explain: Action, the specific steps actually taken, is what most directly demonstrates skills and thinking, and should make up the bulk of the answer, with Situation and Task kept brief.

practice.q: What is the main benefit of preparing a 'story bank' of 5 to 6 flexible stories before an interview?
choices: It guarantees every interview question will be identical
It allows an already-prepared, specific story to be adapted to different questions rather than constructed from scratch under pressure
It eliminates the need to research the company beforehand
It replaces the need for a resume entirely
practice.explain: A small set of well-prepared stories, each adaptable depending on which part is emphasized, covers a wide range of likely behavioral questions without needing to improvise a new story for each one.

lessons.title: Questions to Ask, Research to Do, and Common Mistakes
lessons.intro: An interview is a two-way evaluation, not just a test you're taking. The questions you ask, and how much research clearly went into them, often shape a hiring manager's impression as much as the answers you give.

sections.heading: Researching the Company and Role Beforehand
body: Reviewing the company's website, recent news coverage, and the specific job description line by line before an interview means you can speak concretely about how your background fits the role's actual stated needs, rather than in vague generalities.
Looking up the interviewer's professional background, when it's known in advance, can surface a natural, genuine point of connection or a more informed question to ask them directly.

sections.heading: Good Questions to Ask the Interviewer
body: Specific, informed questions, such as what success looks like in the first 90 days in this role, or what the team's biggest current challenge is, show genuine engagement with the actual job, not just interest in getting any job.

Questions that could have been answered by reading the company's website (basic questions like 'what does your company do') signal that little preparation went into the interview, and tend to leave a weaker impression than more specific, researched questions.

sections.heading: Mistakes That Sink an Otherwise Good Interview
body: Badmouthing a previous employer, even when the criticism feels justified, tends to raise concern about how you'd talk about this employer in a future interview rather than earning sympathy. Arriving with no questions prepared at all often reads as a lack of genuine interest.
Giving vague answers with no specific details, and not knowing basic, easily researched facts about the company, are both common, avoidable mistakes that can outweigh otherwise strong qualifications.

keyTerms.def: Reviewing a company's website, news, and the job description in detail before an interview.
An interview question asking what success looks like in a role's early period, showing genuine engagement.
Arriving at an interview with no questions prepared, often read as low genuine interest.
Looking into an interviewer's professional background in advance, when available, to inform the conversation.

practice.q: Why is asking 'what does success look like in the first 90 days of this role' generally a strong question to ask an interviewer?
choices: Because it's a common phrase that requires no real thought
Because it shows genuine engagement with the actual role and its expectations, rather than a generic question anyone could ask about any job
Because it guarantees a job offer
Because it avoids the need for any other preparation
practice.explain: This question is specific to the role and shows the candidate is thinking concretely about performing well in it, which distinguishes it from a generic or easily-researched question.

practice.q: What impression does badmouthing a previous employer during an interview tend to create, even if the criticism is accurate?
choices: It usually earns sympathy from the interviewer
It tends to raise concern about how the candidate might describe this employer in a future interview
It has no effect on the interviewer's impression
It is generally viewed as a sign of honesty and encouraged
practice.explain: Even accurate criticism of a past employer tends to make an interviewer wonder how they themselves might be described in a future interview, which is why it's generally avoided.

practice.q: Why is arriving at an interview with zero prepared questions considered a mistake?
choices: Because it is against company policy at most organizations
Because it can signal a lack of genuine interest in the specific role
Because interviewers are legally required to ask if you have questions
Because it always shortens the interview significantly
practice.explain: Prepared, specific questions signal genuine engagement with the role; showing up with none can come across as a lack of real interest, regardless of how strong the earlier answers were.

lessons.title: Evaluating and Negotiating a Job Offer
lessons.intro: A job offer's headline salary number is only part of the picture. Two offers with different base salaries can end up worth roughly the same, or even reversed, once benefits and time off are actually accounted for, and negotiating well starts with knowing that full picture.

sections.heading: Total Compensation, Not Just Salary
body: Total compensation includes base salary, any bonus, and the value of benefits: employer retirement contributions or matching, the value of health insurance, and paid time off. A lower base salary paired with a strong retirement match and generous PTO can end up worth more, in real terms, than a higher base salary with neither.

Comparing two offers fairly means adding up this fuller picture, not just glancing at the base salary line, since the base number alone can be misleading about which offer actually provides more overall value.

example.problem: Compare two job offers. Offer A: $58,000 base salary, no 401(k) match, 10 PTO days. Offer B: $54,000 base salary, employer matches 4% of salary into a 401(k), 15 PTO days. Estimate the effective value of each offer's retirement match and compare the offers' rough total value.
steps: Calculate Offer B's 401(k) match value: 4% of $54,000 = $2,160 per year in essentially free retirement contributions.
Add that match to Offer B's base salary for a match-adjusted comparison figure: $54,000 + $2,160 = $56,160.
Compare to Offer A's $58,000 base with no match: Offer A is still nominally higher by about $1,840 in this adjusted comparison.
Factor in the 5 extra PTO days Offer B provides, which have real additional value beyond the dollar figures already compared.
example.answer: Offer A is worth somewhat more in raw, match-adjusted dollars ($58,000 versus $56,160), but Offer B closes most of that gap through its 401(k) match and adds 5 more paid days off, worth weighing directly before deciding based on base salary alone.

sections.heading: How and When to Negotiate
body: Negotiation is generally appropriate after receiving a written offer, not during the interview process itself, when the specific numbers aren't yet formally on the table. Opening with genuine enthusiasm for the role, before raising the number, keeps the conversation collaborative rather than adversarial.

A specific counter-number, backed by something concrete, market rate research, a competing offer, or a specific skill or credential adding value, tends to land far better than a vague request simply for 'more,' which gives the employer nothing concrete to respond to.

sections.heading: A Simple Counter-Offer Script
body: A workable structure: thank them for the offer and express genuine enthusiasm for the role, reference a specific data point (market rate research for the role and location, or a competing offer), name one specific number as the ask, and note openness to discussing further rather than presenting it as a rigid, final demand.

This kind of specific, evidence-based counter tends to be taken seriously precisely because it gives the employer something concrete to evaluate and respond to, unlike a vague, unsupported request for a higher number.

keyTerms.def: The full value of a job offer, including base salary, bonus, and benefits like retirement match and PTO.
An employer's contribution to a retirement account, often a percentage of salary, an addition to base pay's real value.
A specific, evidence-backed request for different compensation terms made after receiving a written job offer.
Data on typical pay for a specific role and location, used to support a negotiation request.

practice.q: An offer includes a $52,000 base salary and a 5% employer 401(k) match. What is the approximate dollar value of that match in the first year?
practice.explain: 5% of $52,000 = $2,600, the approximate annual value of the employer's retirement match, on top of the base salary.

practice.q: When is it generally most appropriate to negotiate salary during a hiring process?
choices: During the very first phone screen, before any offer exists
After receiving a written offer, when specific numbers are formally on the table
Only after starting the job
Negotiation should never be attempted under any circumstances
practice.explain: Negotiating after a written offer is standard practice, since specific numbers are then actually on the table to discuss, rather than negotiating around numbers that haven't been formally proposed yet.

practice.q: Why does a counter-offer backed by specific market rate research tend to be more effective than a vague request for 'more money'?
choices: Because employers are legally required to match researched figures
Because it gives the employer something concrete and evidence-based to evaluate and respond to
Because vague requests are always automatically rejected
There is no real difference in effectiveness between the two approaches
practice.explain: A specific number backed by research or a competing offer gives the employer a concrete basis to evaluate and respond to, unlike an unsupported general request that leaves them nothing specific to react to.

units.title: Thriving in Your First Job and Beyond
units.summary: What actually matters in the first 90 days on a new job, how to build workplace relationships and handle feedback, and how to think about raises and long-term growth.

lessons.title: The First 90 Days: What Actually Matters
lessons.intro: The instinct in a new job is often to prove yourself immediately with a big, visible win. In practice, the first weeks matter more for learning how the team actually works than for delivering something dramatic, and rushing past that learning period tends to backfire.

sections.heading: Learning Before Contributing
body: Every workplace runs on unwritten norms alongside its official policies, who actually makes which decisions, how quickly people expect a reply to a message, which meetings really matter versus which are optional. Learning these norms takes real observation time, and skipping straight to big, independent action before understanding them risks working against the team's actual rhythm rather than fitting into it.
This doesn't mean doing nothing visible in the early weeks, it means prioritizing understanding how work actually gets done here over immediately trying to prove capability with a large solo project.

sections.heading: Building Relationships With Your Manager and Team
body: Regular short check-ins with a manager, even a brief weekly conversation, build a habit of communication before there's ever a problem that requires one. Asking directly how a manager prefers to be updated, brief written summaries versus a quick verbal check-in, avoids guessing at a preference that varies a lot between managers.

Understanding what teammates actually do and how their work connects to yours, beyond just their job title, makes collaboration smoother later and often surfaces who to ask about what before a real deadline crunch makes that knowledge urgent.

sections.heading: Setting Expectations Early
body: Directly asking a manager, in the first weeks, what success looks like at 30, 60, and 90 days removes the guesswork of trying to infer unstated expectations, and gives a concrete target to work toward rather than a vague sense of 'doing well.'

When instructions are genuinely ambiguous, confirming the specific priority directly with a manager, rather than guessing and potentially spending real time on the wrong thing, is almost always the better use of a quick clarifying question.

keyTerms.def: The process of learning a new job's norms, expectations, and ways of working during the early period.
Informal expectations about how work actually happens, distinct from official written policy.
A regular, brief conversation with a manager to maintain communication before a problem requires one.
A concrete set of expectations for what success looks like at each of the first three months in a new role.

practice.q: Why is it generally more effective to prioritize learning a workplace's unwritten norms in the first weeks, rather than immediately attempting a big, independent project?
choices: Because new employees are never allowed to work on real projects
Because working without understanding how the team actually operates risks working against its real rhythm rather than fitting into it
Because unwritten norms are always identical across every workplace
Because managers prefer new employees who do nothing visible for the entire first month
practice.explain: Skipping the learning period and jumping straight to big independent action risks misjudging how decisions and priorities actually work on this specific team, since those unwritten norms vary by workplace.

practice.q: What is a practical benefit of asking a manager directly, in the first weeks, what success looks like at 30, 60, and 90 days?
choices: It guarantees a raise at the 90-day mark
It replaces the need for any further check-ins
It removes the guesswork of inferring unstated expectations and provides a concrete target to work toward
It is only useful for managerial roles, not entry-level ones
practice.explain: A direct, concrete answer about expectations at specific milestones gives a clear target to work toward, rather than guessing at what 'doing well' might mean.

practice.q: When instructions from a manager are genuinely ambiguous, what is generally the better approach?
choices: Guessing at the intended priority and proceeding without asking
Confirming the specific priority directly with the manager before spending significant time on the task
Waiting for the manager to notice and clarify on their own
Asking a different teammate to decide instead
practice.explain: A brief clarifying question up front is almost always a better use of time than proceeding on a guess that could turn out to be the wrong priority entirely.

lessons.title: Receiving Feedback and Workplace Professionalism
lessons.intro: Critical feedback in a new job can feel like a verdict on whether you belong there. Treated instead as specific information about what to adjust, the same feedback becomes something genuinely useful rather than something to simply survive.

sections.heading: Feedback Is Information, Not a Verdict
body: Reacting to critical feedback with the growth mindset covered in this course's earlier lessons on mindset, treating it as specific, actionable information rather than a judgment of overall worth, changes what happens next. A defensive reaction tends to shut down the conversation before the actually useful part, what specifically to do differently, ever gets discussed.
Asking a direct, specific clarifying question, 'can you give me an example of what that would look like done differently,' turns vague feedback into something concrete enough to actually act on.

sections.heading: Email, Meetings, and Everyday Professionalism
body: Prompt, clear replies to work email, even a brief acknowledgment when a full answer will take longer, signal reliability. Arriving prepared and on time to meetings, having reviewed any materials sent in advance, shows respect for other people's time, which is noticed more than it might seem.

Communication norms vary meaningfully between workplaces, some are highly formal, others casual, and matching the specific norms of your particular workplace, rather than assuming one universal standard applies everywhere, is part of professionalism itself.

sections.heading: Handling Disagreement Productively
body: Raising a concern directly and respectfully with the person actually involved, rather than only discussing it with others, resolves more issues and avoids the appearance of going around someone. Focusing specifically on the issue and its concrete impact, rather than on personal criticism, keeps a disagreement productive rather than personal.

This mirrors the attribution principle from earlier study skills content: framing a disagreement around a specific, changeable action ('this approach caused a delay') rather than a fixed trait ('you're careless') makes the conversation about a fixable problem rather than a character attack.

keyTerms.def: Specific, actionable information about performance, best treated as information rather than a personal verdict.
The communication style and expectations specific to a particular workplace, which vary between organizations.
Reliable, respectful conduct in everyday workplace interactions like email and meetings.
Raising a concern respectfully with the person actually involved, rather than only discussing it with others.

practice.q: What is the recommended way to respond to critical feedback at work?
choices: Treat it as a personal verdict and become defensive
Treat it as specific, actionable information, asking a clarifying question if needed to make it concrete
Ignore it unless it's repeated multiple times
Only accept feedback from senior managers
practice.explain: Treating feedback as specific, changeable information, and asking for concrete examples when needed, makes it usable, whereas a defensive reaction tends to shut down the useful part of the conversation.

practice.q: Why does the lesson emphasize that communication norms vary between workplaces?
choices: Because there is one universal professional standard that applies everywhere
Because matching the specific norms of a particular workplace, rather than assuming a single fixed standard, is itself part of professionalism
Because formal workplaces are always superior to casual ones
Communication norms have no real effect on how professionalism is perceived
practice.explain: Since formality and communication style genuinely differ between organizations, adapting to the specific workplace's actual norms, rather than applying one assumed standard everywhere, is part of behaving professionally.

practice.q: Which framing of a workplace disagreement is most likely to keep the conversation productive?
choices: 'You're careless and don't pay attention to detail.'
'This specific approach caused a two-day delay on the project; can we adjust the process for next time?'
Avoiding the conversation and complaining to other coworkers instead
Waiting until a performance review to mention it
practice.explain: Focusing on a specific, changeable action and its concrete impact keeps the conversation about a fixable problem, rather than framing it as a fixed personal trait, which tends to provoke defensiveness.

lessons.title: Raises, Promotions, and Long-Term Career Growth
lessons.intro: Asking for a raise with nothing more specific to say than 'I've been here a while' rarely succeeds. Asking with a documented record of specific accomplishments and their measurable impact is a fundamentally different, and far stronger, conversation.

sections.heading: When to Ask for a Raise
body: A raise conversation lands strongest after a clear, documented pattern of added responsibility or measurable results, not simply after a fixed amount of time has passed with no particular change in contribution. Timing the conversation around a performance review cycle, when compensation decisions are already actively being considered, also tends to work in a candidate's favor.

This doesn't mean tenure is irrelevant, but tenure alone, without a case for added value delivered during that time, is a much weaker argument than tenure paired with specific, demonstrated growth in responsibility or results.

sections.heading: Making the Case With Evidence
body: Keeping an ongoing, running record of specific accomplishments and their measurable impact throughout the year, rather than trying to reconstruct everything from memory right before the conversation, produces a far stronger and more complete case when the time comes to actually ask.

Leading with the most quantifiable, business-relevant items, ones tied to revenue, cost savings, or time saved, generally makes a stronger opening than a long, undifferentiated list of every task performed.

example.problem: An employee wants a raise and has kept a running list of accomplishments this year: led onboarding for 3 new hires, cut weekly report preparation time from 3 hours to 45 minutes by building a template, and led a project that generated $12,000 in new revenue. Turn this into a strong opening statement for a raise conversation.
steps: Identify the most quantifiable, business-relevant items first: the $12,000 revenue project and the time saved on reporting.
Convert the time savings into a clear value statement: reducing report prep from 3 hours to 45 minutes saves about 2.25 hours per week, roughly 117 hours over a year.
Combine the two or three strongest points into one concise opening statement, rather than listing every task performed.

Draft the statement: 'Over the past year I led onboarding for 3 new hires, built a reporting template that saves about 117 hours a year of team time, and led a project that generated $12,000 in new revenue. I'd like to talk about adjusting my compensation to reflect that.'
example.answer: Leading with the two most quantifiable, business-relevant contributions, dollar impact and hours saved, makes a substantially stronger opening case than a general list of duties performed, since it gives the manager concrete, defensible numbers to work with.

sections.heading: Thinking Beyond the Next Raise
body: Periodically reassessing whether a current role and company still fit your longer-term growth, rather than only evaluating it at the moment a frustration arises, keeps career decisions deliberate rather than reactive.

Building skills that would transfer to a different role or company, and keeping the professional network built in unit 2 warm even while currently employed, both protect against being caught without options if circumstances at a current job change unexpectedly.

keyTerms.def: The recurring period when a company formally evaluates performance and considers compensation changes.
An ongoing, running record of specific achievements and their measurable impact, kept throughout the year.
A change to salary or other pay, typically requested based on demonstrated added value.
Long-term development of skills, responsibility, and options, extending beyond any single raise or promotion.

practice.q: Why does keeping an ongoing accomplishment log throughout the year produce a stronger raise conversation than trying to recall achievements right before asking?
choices: Because managers require a written log by policy
Because a running record captures specific, measurable accomplishments as they happen, rather than relying on incomplete memory later
Because logs are only useful for annual performance reviews, not raise requests
There is no real difference between the two approaches
practice.explain: An ongoing log captures specific details and numbers while they're fresh, producing a more complete and credible case than trying to reconstruct a year of accomplishments from memory just before the conversation.

practice.q: An employee reduces a weekly task from 3 hours to 1 hour. Approximately how many hours per year does this save (assuming a 50-week work year)?
choices: 50 hours
100 hours
150 hours
200 hours
practice.explain: The time saved per week is 3 − 1 = 2 hours. Over 50 weeks: 2 × 50 = 100 hours saved per year.

practice.q: According to this lesson, why is timing alone, such as 'I've worked here for two years,' generally a weaker argument for a raise than a documented record of added value?
choices: Because tenure is completely irrelevant to any raise decision
Because tenure without a demonstrated case for added responsibility or measurable results is a much weaker argument than tenure paired with specific evidence of growth
Because raises are never based on time at a company under any circumstances
Because performance review cycles ignore tenure entirely
practice.explain: Tenure alone doesn't demonstrate increased value delivered; pairing time at the company with specific, measurable contributions makes for a substantially stronger case.
